Scaling AI Infrastructure with Integrated Optics
Near Margalit
Vice President and General Manager, Optical Systems Division
Optics
AI Infrastructure
Share:

As copper interconnects reach their physical reach and power limits at higher data rates, next-generation AI data centers require a new approach to scaling compute. Integrated optics provides the path forward, overcoming electrical bottlenecks to deliver the reach, power efficiency, and density needed for scale-up interconnects.

Integrated Optics

Copper interconnects, driven by SerDes cores integrated inside ASICs, are no longer able to keep pace with the bandwidth, data rate, and physical density requirements of next-generation AI data center interconnects. Interconnect bandwidth for AI is expected to roughly double every year, requiring a corresponding doubling in per-lane data rates.  But higher data rates come at the cost of reach.  

At the same time, to optimize compute cost and physical area, new XPU architectures are increasing the number of XPUs per rack and pushing required interconnect reach well beyond 2 meters.  The power needed to compensate for copper losses at these higher data rates no longer fits within allocated power budgets, where power must go to compute, not signal integrity.

Integrated optics overcomes the reach and power limits of copper at these higher rates while matching its reliability and cost, enabling a multi-generational, multi-segment interconnect roadmap.  Short reach next-generation AI links span three tiers: Scale-Out, Scale-Up, and most recently Scale-In:

Scale-Out interconnects, those between racks and clusters, are still served mostly by pluggable optical modules with increasingly advanced integration of optics and components, but On-Board Optics (OBO), Near-Package Optics (NPO), and Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) continue to demonstrate significant power, cost, and reliability advantages.  
Scale-up interconnects, those within a rack, are rapidly moving toward larger domain sizes and disaggregation, where Optical Compute Interconnects (OCI) are enabling next-generation deployments.  
Scale-In interconnects, those within XPUs inside a single server tray, are exploring next generation packaging technologies and further optical integration.  
Click to enlarge image
Figure 1. Scale-Out, Scale-up, and Scale-in Interconnects
PAM-4 vs PAM-6

As data rates push to 400G/lane, copper losses severely limit reach at PAM-4 modulation.  Moving to 400G PAM-6 increases the transmission distance through copper but if interconnects are needed for more than 2-3m, optical interconnects will be required.  

Think of the total optical power budget as a small fixed-height ruler.  PAM-4 modulation divides that ruler in 4 brightness levels: 3 gaps between them, each gap 1/3 of the ruler.  Each of these gaps encodes the signal with a “1” or “0” so you can have (23) eight combinations.  PAM-6 divides the same ruler into 6 levels, 5 gaps, each 1/5 of the ruler, (25) thirty two combinations.  The slicer inside the SerDes core must decide whether each gap is a “1” or a “0” by finding a mid-point in the eye and slicing the eye at that point to make the determination.  

Smaller gaps between the levels means less room for noise before the SerDes misreads the level.  The room for noise is called signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) margin and going from PAM-4 to PAM-6 at 400 Gbps costs roughly 5-7dB of required SNR.  Optical links already run with tighter signal margin than electrical ones and this additional 5-7 dB penalty is why optics at PAM-6 isn’t the efficient choice even though it looks more attractive on paper packing more data per symbol.  See Figure 1. below, the eye diagrams are from simulations.1

Click to enlarge image
PAM-4 vs PAM-6
Converting the Signal

We can still use 400G PAM-4 for optics, the issue is how do we convert a 400G PAM-6 electrical signal to a 400G PAM-4 optical signal or how can we get enough reach from electrical links at 400G PAM-4 to directly drive the optics.  For the latter, the industry is looking to integrated optics with OBO, NPO, and CPO to extend the reach of electrical signals at 400G PAM-4 that can then directly drive optics at 400G PAM-4.  

For the former, a gearbox is required to convert the PAM-6 electrical signal into a PAM-4 optical signal which requires additional power that should be allocated to compute.  To deploy the first 400G/lane systems early adopters will use a gearbox to convert the PAM-6 electrical signal into a PAM-4 optical signal.  However, this approach requires a significant amount of additional power that would otherwise be allocated to compute.  As technology matures the industry will look to integrated optics using OBO, NPO, or CPO to extend the reach of electrical signals at 400G PAM-4 to then directly drive optics at 400G PAM-4.

What Happens Next?

We can potentially move to 800G PAM-4 but this will incur severe power penalties, new material structures, and less efficient architectures.   We can move to higher order modulation with coherent technologies, but these systems require heavy overhead, timing, and local oscillators which make it difficult to deploy at the cost and power requirements for scale-up interconnects.

We must first decouple the CMOS electrical lane rate from the silicon modulator and waveguide optical lane rate.  An optical waveguide can transmit many wavelengths simultaneously using wavelength division multiplexing (WDM).   A system could now transmit 32 wavelengths at 100 Gbps, 3.2 Tbps, versus the same system using 1 wavelength at 100 Gbps!  

As we can now scale bandwidth with optical wavelengths as opposed to dense copper lanes, we no longer need higher data rate, higher order modulation electrical lane rates.  We can also reduce the electrical lane rate to 50 Gbps, non-return to zero (NRZ) instead of using Phase Amplitude Modulation (PAM).  Unlike PAM, NRZ is a single EYE with relaxed SNR budgets.

This does several things:

It provides a renewed multigenerational path to scale electrical lane rates moving from 50 Gbps NRZ to 100 Gbps NRZ
It reduces the requirements on link budget while drastically reducing power and improving link performance
It reduces latency by enabling the use of lower Forward Error Correction (FEC) coding and interleaving.  

All of these provide the right platform to bring optics into the scale-up domain.

Click to enlarge image
Figure 3. Measured OCI-MSA GEN1 53.125 Gbps NRZ Transmit EYE
Optical Compute Interconnect (OCI) Multi-Source Agreement (MSA)

In order to address larger single-node domain sizes, power per rack and cooling limitations, increased cabling complexity and costs, and physical reach limits the OCI-MSA was founded in March of 2026 by AMD, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Nvidia to standardize an optical interconnect for Scale-up links moving single node compute to multi-node in row compute.

The Gen 1 specification has been published using 53.125 Gbps NRZ electrical signaling and a dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) wavelength grid with cascaded micro-ring resonators (MRR) at ~2.3nm spacing.  Figure 3 above shows the industry’s first measured OCI-MSA transmitter eye using Micro-Ring Resonators (MRM) on Broadcom silicon running at 53.125 Gbps NRZ. Each optical fiber can support 212.5 Gbps bi-direction with 4 DWDM wavelengths at 53.125 Gbps, transmitting 4 𝞴 per fiber per direction on current industry standard Corse wavelength-division multiplexing (CWDM) wavelength groups for the transmitter and the receiver.  Figure 4 below is a specification drawing from the OCI-GEN1 specification that can be downloaded from the OCI-MSA.org website.

Click to enlarge image
Figure 4. DWDM wavelength channels on CWDM wavelength groups for a Bi-Di link

As we move beyond this, maintaining the same wavelength spacing: Gen2 at 400 Gbps per fiber, 4 DWDM wavelengths at 103.25 Gbps, Gen3, at 800 Gbps per fiber, 8 DWDM wavelengths at 103.25 Gbps and beyond, we ensure the use of standard Continuous Wave (CW) laser sources. The WDM roadmap can continue to extend this to 3.2T Gbps per fiber, well beyond the current projected need of scale-up interconnects.

Bi-Di Technology

In May of 2024, well before anyone else, Broadcom published a white paper on the use of bi-directional (Bi-Di) technology for AI/ML clusters using optics for GPU clusters of 512 and 1024.  The paper showed that comparing traditional DR-based optics vs. Bi-Di technology reduces the number of fibers needed by 50%, lowers the cost of optics by as much at 15%, and enables more efficient ways to construct scale-up networks.3   We have carried that technology forward and implemented it into the OCI-MSA.

Implementation

Finally, integrated optics comes down to implementation.  As a founding member of the OCI-MSA we understand the importance of supporting an open ecosystem where the industry can benefit from economies of scale with a unified approach for scale-up optical interconnect.  

All the implementation options shown below in Figure 5 below can be used by the industry and innovated upon to deliver optics into the scale-up domain at volume.  Fundamentally, optics needs to be at the same reliability, power, and cost as today’s copper interconnects.  We have been working on a solution to replace the copper SerDes with an optical SerDes that would be placed directly on the interposer to achieve this parity with copper links, and as we have shown above, enable a new roadmap for bandwidth growth.  We are currently working on this technology and expect to bring it to market within the next year.
